readerTitle: Why the smaller number wins the pitch
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 청소 서비스, 레스토랑 2호점) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 피치는 큰 숫자로 설득하는 것이 아니라, 듣는 사람이 한 단계씩 확인할 수 있는 작은 숫자의 사슬로 설득한다. 투자자는 가장 약한 고리를 본다.
misconception: 시장 규모가 클수록, 그리고 '1%만 가져가도'라고 말할수록 피치가 강해진다.

sources.text: 창업·투자 실무에서 널리 쓰이는 원칙 (하향식 시장 추정보다 상향식 추정 선호, 금액과 마일스톤을 연결한 투자 요청)

factChecks.note: '1% of a huge market' 논리를 투자자들이 불신한다는 점은 업계에서 널리 공유되는 관행적 견해이며, 특정 연구 결과로 제시하지 않았습니다. 카드 문장도 일반론으로만 썼습니다.
레스토랑 문제의 수치(주 900 커버, 손익분기 600 커버, $400,000)는 가상이며 서로 계산 관계를 주장하지 않습니다. 손익분기는 '가정에 따라'로 명시했습니다.

cards.title: Why the smaller number wins the pitch
body: Two founders pitch the same angel investor. Both run home-cleaning businesses.
The first says: "Home cleaning is a $10 billion market. We only need 1%." The second says: "4,000 homes in our area already pay for cleaning. We serve 60 of them."
One number is over a thousand times bigger. The investor backs the smaller one.

image.label: Two pitch slides: a giant number and a small, specific one
image.brief: 두 장의 발표 슬라이드가 나란히. 왼쪽은 거대한 "$10B" 글자가 흐릿하게 떠 있고, 오른쪽은 작은 동네 지도 위에 집 아이콘 60개가 선명하게 표시됨. 투자자 실루엣이 오른쪽으로 몸을 기울임. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: How do you show the size of the opportunity?
body: You run a home-cleaning service and you're asking a local angel for $150,000. You have one slide to show how big this could get.

options.text: The national market size, and that you only need 1% of it
options.feedback: It sounds big and safe, but it says nothing about how you'd win even one customer. Any competitor could show the same slide.

options.text: Homes in your area that already pay for cleaning, times what they spend, and how many you serve today
options.feedback: Smaller number, but every part can be checked. The investor can follow it from your street to your forecast.

options.text: Your story of why you started, with no numbers yet
options.feedback: A good story earns attention, but it leaves the investor to guess the size. Keep the story and add the numbers behind it.

cards.title: Build the number from the ground up.
body: Each line is something the investor can check or question. The goal of 400 homes is 10% of the area, which earns **$720,000 a year**. Far smaller than $100 million, and far easier to believe.

breakdown.label: Homes in reach
breakdown.detail: Already pay for cleaning in your service area

cards.title: The pitch
body: A **pitch** is a short argument that walks a listener from a problem to a specific request. Each step has to be believable on its own.
The usual steps: who has the problem, what you do about it, why you, what has happened so far, the numbers, and the ask.
Here's the twist. Listeners judge the chain by its **weakest link**. A giant number nobody can check doesn't strengthen the pitch. It becomes the weak link.

image.label: A chain of six links, one cracked
image.brief: 가로로 이어진 쇠사슬 고리 6개에 각각 "Problem", "Solution", "Why you", "Proof", "Numbers", "Ask" 라벨. "Numbers" 고리만 금이 가 있고 돋보기가 그 고리를 비춤.

cards.title: Answer the next question before it's asked.
body: Every claim in a pitch raises a question in the listener's head. A strong pitch answers it on the next slide.
list: **Problem:** who has it, and how do you know?
**Solution:** why does this work better than what they do now?
**Proof:** what has already happened, not just what might?
**Numbers:** are they built from customers and prices?
**Ask:** how much, for what, and until which milestone?
cards.softwareNote: "1% of all small businesses worldwide" is weaker than "8,000 dental clinics in our region use paper scheduling, 30 pay us $99 a month." Seats, price and current users make the chain checkable.

cards.title: Tie the money to a milestone.
body: "We're raising $150,000" leaves the investor wondering what it buys.
"$150,000 hires and equips two more crews. That takes us from 60 to 400 homes in about two years" connects the ask to the chain above it.
Now the investor isn't judging a dream. They're judging whether one step leads to the next.

image.label: Money bag with an arrow to a milestone flag
image.brief: 돈주머니 "$150K"에서 화살표가 청소 팀 두 개 아이콘을 거쳐 "400 homes" 깃발로 이어지는 단순한 흐름도. 밝은 색감, 실제 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: A clear pitch can't fix a weak business.
body: Ground-up numbers can be inflated too. If you assume every nearby home will sign up, the math is neat and still wrong. Say which assumptions you've tested and which you haven't.
And clarity cuts both ways. A pitch that hides the weak link may win money you'll struggle to repay. The investor will find the weak link eventually. Better that you find it first.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant.
body: Your first restaurant is busy. You want $400,000 from local investors to open a second site. Which ask slide is strongest?

options.text: "We're raising $400,000 to grow. Full financials are in the appendix."
options.feedback: Honest and complete, but it makes the investor dig for the link between money and result. Most won't.

options.text: "$400,000 builds and opens site two. Site one serves 900 covers a week; site two breaks even at about 600, on these assumptions."
options.feedback: Money, milestone and proof sit in one line. The investor can test each assumption instead of guessing.

options.text: "Dining out in our city is a $2 billion market. Site two needs only a sliver."
options.feedback: It sounds safe but tells the investor nothing about this site. It also hints that you haven't done the site-level math.

cards.title: A pitch is only as strong as its weakest step.
body: Build your numbers from real customers and prices, and tie your ask to a milestone. Small and checkable beats big and vague.
**Try it today:** write your opportunity in one line: customers in reach × what they pay × how many you have now. Circle the number you're least sure of.
